Fit LPPLS Model to Financial Time Series

Source: R/lppls_fitter.R
fit_lppls.Rd

Fits the Log-Periodic Power Law Singularity (LPPLS) model to log-price data using the calibration methods from Filimonov & Sornette (2013). Supports multiple optimization modes and provides diagnostic outputs.

Usage

fit_lppls(
  log_price,
  fh = 30,
  hold_out = 0,
  lower = c(0.1, 6, -1e+14, 0.8),
  upper = c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e+06),
  tc_init = 1000,
  m_init = 0.5,
  o_init = 13,
  num_searches = 20,
  mode = "F2",
  mpl_plot = FALSE,
  mpl_cutoff = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5),
  fp = FALSE,
  cp = FALSE,
  sp = FALSE,
  tp = c(0, 0, 0),
  tp_id = 1,
  pp = FALSE,
  mp = FALSE,
  factr = 1e+07,
  fb = FALSE,
  beta_method = c("crossprod", "qr", "chol", "symengine"),
  dates = NULL,
  style = c("simulated", "empirical"),
  data_label = NULL
)

Arguments

log_price

Numeric vector of log-prices.

fh

Integer, forecast horizon length in time units (default 30). The search for tc extends from T2+1 to T2+fh where fh>1.

hold_out

Integer, number of observations to hold out from the end of the sample for validation (default 0). That is, the number of data points after T2.

lower

Numeric vector of length 4, lower bounds for c(m, omega, B, D). Default: c(0.1, 6, -1e14, 0.8).
The defaults of lower and upper follow the constraints of Filimonov, Demos & Sornette (2017): \(B < 0\), \(D \geq 0.8\), \(0.1 \leq m \leq 0.9\) and \(6 \leq \omega \leq 13\), which they give as approximate. The damping bound relaxes the theoretical \(D > 1\), which keeps the crash hazard rate non-negative (Graf v. Bothmer & Meister, 2003), because a real crash unfolds over weeks rather than in one immediate jump.
NOTE: For trace_plot mode 2 and 3 (bm and bo), lower for B should be set to the desired minimum value of the B-axis in the contour plotting.
Example:

lower = c(0.1, 6, -0.03, 0.8)

If the optimization algorithm goes below the lower limits at any point the lower limit for the B-axis will be extended automatically.

upper

Numeric vector of length 4, upper bounds for c(m, omega, B, D). Default: c(0.9, 13, -1e-14, 1e6).

tc_init

Numeric, initial value of critical time tc for optim() (default 1000). tc_init should be in \([T_2+1, T_3]\), where \(T_3 = T_2 + s\), and \(s\) is the forecast horizon.

m_init

Numeric, initial value of power law exponent m for optim() (default 0.5). m_init should be in [lower[1], upper[1]]. The algorithm will search for initial values of m and omega that give B<0. If such values are found, the given init values will be overwritten.

o_init

Numeric, initial value of frequency omega for optim() (default 13). o_init should be in [lower[2], upper[2]]. Default is 13, which increases the probability of B<0 (of course not for random initial values). The algorithm will search for initial values of m and omega that give B<0. If such values are found, the given init values will be overwritten.

num_searches

Integer, number of times to repeat the optimization wrt tc, m and omega. First iteration uses given initial values. Any subsequent iterations use random initial values. In modes "F2" and "MPL" these are seeded internally, so the result does not depend on the state of the random number generator, and the caller's random number stream is left as it was. In mode "F1" they are drawn from the caller's stream.

mode

Character, optimization mode:

F1

Optimize wrt tc, m, omega simultaneously

F2

Optimize wrt m, omega first (for each tc), then optimize wrt tc

MPL

Modified Profile Likelihood with likelihood intervals

mpl_plot

Logical, whether to generate MPL plot (default FALSE).

mpl_cutoff

Numeric vector of length 3, cutoff levels (\(c\)) for likelihood interval (default c(0.05, 0.1, 0.5)). See Filimonov2017 equation (39). \(c = 0.05\) indicates that values of tc outside the likelihood interval have a probability of 0.05.

fp

Logical, whether to generate fit plot (default FALSE).

cp

Logical, whether to generate contour plot (default FALSE). tc value is fixed to the estimate with the lowest objective function value.

sp

Logical, whether to generate surface plot (default FALSE). tc value is fixed to the estimate with the lowest objective function value.

tp

Numeric vector of length 3, 0/1 selectors for trace plots. Plot 1: m-omega, plot 2: B-m, plot 3:B-omega (default c(0, 0, 0)).
Example: c(1, 0, 1) selects trace plot 1 and 3. Traces convergence of parameters during optimization of F2 objective function. Only works when mode = "F2". The plotted trace path is the one for the value of tc that produced the smallest value of SSE2.
NOTE: Contour plots in trace plot 2 and 3 only apply to the first step in the trace. In a trace plot wrt B and m, omega is not fixed (and vice versa for m and omega).

tp_id

Integer, which trace step to use for contour plot (default 1). If the indicated id is too high, 1 will be chosen.

pp

Logical, whether to generate parameter plot (default FALSE).

mp

Logical, whether to generate matrix plot (default FALSE). x-axis is tc, y-axis is SSE. 3 columns of plots for smallest and biggest value of m, and value between the two. 3 columns of plots for smallest and biggest value of omega, and value between the two.

factr

Numeric, convergence tolerance for the L-BFGS-B control list (default 1e7, which is also stats::optim()'s own default). It is a multiplier on machine epsilon, not an absolute tolerance: the optimiser stops when the relative reduction in the objective falls below factr * .Machine$double.eps, so 1e7 asks for roughly 1e-9.

Smaller is not automatically better. Any value below about 1e0 requests a tolerance finer than double precision can represent, which cannot be satisfied: L-BFGS-B then runs until its line search fails and returns convergence code 52 rather than converging. Earlier versions of this package defaulted to 1e-08, which requests 2.2e-24 and had exactly that effect – about five times more objective evaluations than 1e7, ending in line-search failure for two thirds of the candidate tc values, and reaching the same optimum. See misc/bench_beta.Rmd for the measurements.

fb

Logical, whether to print feedback during execution (default FALSE).

beta_method

Character, how to solve for the linear parameters \(A, B, C_1, C_2\) given \((t_c, m, \omega)\).

At fixed \((t_c, m, \omega)\) the model is linear in those four coefficients, so with \(\tau = t_c - t\) it is \(y = X\beta\) for the \(n \times 4\) design matrix $$X = [\,1,\; \tau^{m},\; \tau^{m}\cos(\omega \log \tau),\; \tau^{m}\sin(\omega \log \tau)\,],\qquad \beta = (A, B, C_1, C_2)'$$ whose columns are linearly independent for \(m \ne 0\), \(\omega \ne 0\). Every method returns the same \(\hat\beta = \arg\min_\beta \|y - X\beta\|^2\) and differs only in how it is computed. The solver runs once per objective evaluation, so it dominates the cost of a calibration.

"crossprod"

(default) Normal equations, \((X'X)\hat\beta = X'y\), via crossprod() and solve(). Fastest: \(X\) is built once and the residuals are formed as \(y - X\hat\beta\), so the series is walked a single time. Exact to well within anything interpretable over the admissible \(0.1 \le m \le 0.9\).

"qr"

Householder QR of \(X\) via .lm.fit(), which yields the residuals as part of the factorisation, so the fitted values are never reconstructed. Never forms \(X'X\), and since \(\kappa_2(X'X) = \kappa_2(X)^2\) it does not square the condition number. About 30% slower and markedly more accurate; prefer it if lower[1] is widened toward \(m \to 0\), where \(\tau^{m} \to 1\) rotates into the intercept column and \(X\) approaches rank deficiency.

"chol"

Cholesky factorisation of \(X'X\), which is symmetric positive definite whenever \(X\) has full column rank.

"symengine"

The thesis implementation: the \(4 \times 4\) system is solved symbolically once and compiled to one closure per coefficient, fed by hand-computed entries of \(X'X\) and \(X'y\). Retained so the thesis calibration can be reproduced and inspected directly – it is roughly ten times slower than the default and the least accurate of the four.

The methods are not bit-identical to one another. The three numerical solvers evaluate the objective in a single pass over the series, which is also not bit-identical to a two-pass evaluation of the same solve: forming the fitted values as \(X\hat\beta\) sums the four terms in a different order than re-evaluating \(A + \tau^{m}(B + C_1\cos(\omega\log\tau) + C_2\sin(\omega\log\tau))\) from the closed form. The differences are at the level of the last few significant digits and do not move any reported quantity, but they mean a calibration is bit-reproducible only against the same beta_method.

See misc/bench_beta.Rmd for the timings and precision measurements behind these characterisations.

dates

NULL (default) or a Date vector the same length as log_price, strictly increasing, labelling the 1..n time index with calendar dates. Purely presentational: the calibration is index-based and its results do not depend on dates. When supplied, the attached fit plot is drawn on a calendar axis, and print() and summary() report \(\hat{t}_c\), the MPLE and every likelihood interval as dates as well as indices. A forecast critical time beyond the end of the series is extrapolated at the series' median spacing and flagged with *.

style

One of "simulated" (default) or "empirical", passed to fit_plot() for the attached fit plot. "empirical" draws an observed series in grey and splits the fitted curve at T2, so the forecast beyond the calibration window is marked in red. See fit_plot().

data_label

NULL (default) or a string naming the observed series in the attached fit plot's legend. The default follows style.

Value

A list containing:

fit

List with fitted model results. In F1/F2 mode:

mode = "F1"

List of fits with random initial values.

fit[[1]]

list of best fit coefficients optimized wrt m and omega.

fit[[2]]

Tibble of fits with random starting parameters.
Sorted by objective function value (best at top).
Output format:


                [
                  list(tc, m, omega, A, B, C1, C2, D, value_min, ID),
                  list(tc, m, omega, A, B, C1, C2, D, value, ID),
                  ...,
                  list(tc, m, omega, A, B, C1, C2, D, value_max, ID)
                ]
fit[[3]]

If no fits passed the filter: Only unfiltered fits returned.

ID is an identifier indicating the order pre-sorting. These are the indexes reported in "out of range" warnings.

mode = "F2"

List with two or three elements:

fit[[1]]

List of best fit coefficients optimized wrt m and omega.

fit[[2]]

If at least one fit passed the filter: Tibble of best fits for objective function F2 for each value of tc. Columns are: c(ID, value, tc, m, omega, A, B, C1, C2, damp). Sorted by objective function value (best at top). For each value of tc the best fit is picked from that tc's table in fit[[4]].
If no fits passed the filter: Only unfiltered fits returned.

fit[[3]]

If at least one fit passed the filter: Unfiltered fits returned.
If no fits passed the filter: Nothing is returned in fit[[3]]

fit[[4]]

List of all tmp fits
For each tc value, there is a tibble with all fits using random starting points.

mpl_output

(MPL mode only) List with likelihood intervals, R values, log-likelihoods
mpl = list(LI, R, LL, MLL)

LI

vector of 3 elements, one for each value of mpl_cutoff.

R

number, relative likelihood

LL

vector of MPL log-likelihoods for each tc value

MLL

maximum of LL

tc_hat_mpl

tc for which LL takes it's maximum

mpl_plot

(if requested) ggplot2 object for Modified Profile Likelihood plot with likelihood intervals

fit_plot

(if requested) ggplot2 object for fit plot

contour_data

(if requested) List with x, y and z data for contour plot of SSE wrt m and omega.

contour_plot

(if requested) plotly object for contour plot

surface_plot

(if requested) plotly object for surface plot

trace_plot_mo

(if requested) ggplot2 object containing trace plot for m and omega

trace_plot_bm

(if requested) ggplot2 object containing trace plot for B and m

trace_plot_bo

(if requested) ggplot2 object for containing trace plot for B and omega

param_plot

(if requested) ggplot2 object for parameter plot

matrix_plot

(if requested) ggplot2 object for matrix plot

out_of_range_tracker

List tracking which fits had out-of-range B or damping values

F1 mode

List of random iteration IDs what resulted in out-of-range parameters

F2 mode

List of random tc value IDs and iteration IDs what resulted in out-of-range parameters.
tc value ID start with 1 for T2+1. That is, the first time step after the modelling period, or the first time step of the forecasting horizon.

log_price

The input series, so diagnostics that need the data do not make the caller supply it again. The calibration slice is log_price[seq_len(fit_args$n)].

fit_args

List recording the settings this calibration ran with – mode, n (calibration length), fh, hold_out, lower, upper, num_searches and mpl_cutoff. Diagnostics need these: whether m = 0.9 is a boundary solution or an interior optimum cannot be told from the estimate alone.

The list has class "lppls_fit". A calibration can look convincing as a plot and still not be worth interpreting, so the object carries its own diagnostics:

print.lppls_fit()

Printing the fit reports the estimate together with the checks that decide whether to trust it – bounds, optimisation basins, search filters and the extent of the modified profile likelihood. Warnings are listed only when something is wrong.

summary.lppls_fit()

The same as values rather than text, plus the curvature check and whether each likelihood interval is closed by the likelihood or by the edge of the tc grid.

plot.lppls_fit()

Any plot attached at fit time, or the basin views, drawn on demand.

lppls_curvature()

Whether the estimate sits at a genuine interior minimum, which is what the modified profile likelihood assumes.

Details

The LPPLS model is: $$y(t) = A + (t_c - t)^m [B + C_1 \cos(\omega \log(t_c - t)) + C_2 \sin(\omega \log(t_c - t))]$$

The model has 7 parameters: \(A\), \(B\), \(C_1\), \(C_2\) (linear) and \(t_c\), \(m\), \(\omega\) (nonlinear). The Filimonov calibration exploits this structure by solving for the linear parameters analytically given the nonlinear ones.

Mode F1: Optimizes all nonlinear parameters c(tc, m, omega) simultaneously using L-BFGS-B with multiple random starting points.

Mode F2: A two-stage procedure:

  1. For each candidate tc value, optimize c(m, omega)

  2. Select the tc that minimizes the overall SSE

This is more robust than F1 for ill-conditioned problems.

Mode MPL: Modified Profile Likelihood inference from Filimonov et al. (2017). Provides likelihood-based confidence intervals for tc.

Profiling mode = "MPL" on macOS

Running a sampling profiler over an MPL calibration can crash the R session ("Illegal instruction: 4") on macOS builds that use Apple's Accelerate framework as their BLAS – which is the default for the CRAN macOS build of R. This affects utils::Rprof() and everything layered on it (profvis, the RStudio profiler, proftools).

The fault is an interaction between R's profiler and Accelerate's DGEMM, not a fault in this package: it reproduces in plain R with no packages loaded, via Rprof(tempfile()); for (i in 1:2e5) crossprod(A, B) for matrices A, B of a few hundred rows or more. MPL mode is the only part of lpplsF that reaches it, because the modified profile likelihood is the only place that multiplies two matrices; every other product here is a one-argument crossprod(), a matrix-vector product or a decomposition, none of which are affected. Fitting itself is unaffected – the crash requires a profiler to be running.

To profile MPL mode, take R's own matrix products instead of the BLAS for the duration of the profiling session:

old <- options(matprod = "internal")
Rprof("prof.out")
fit <- fit_lppls(log_price, mode = "MPL", ...)
Rprof(NULL)
options(old)
summaryRprof("prof.out")

matprod = "internal" costs only a few percent on a whole MPL fit, since the fit does relatively few matrix-matrix products. It does sum in a different order, so estimates move in the last couple of digits; that is immaterial for a profiling run but is a reason not to set it globally.

References

Filimonov, V., & Sornette, D. (2013). A stable and robust calibration scheme of the log-periodic power law model. Physica A, 392(17), 3698-3707.

Filimonov, V., Demos, G., & Sornette, D. (2017). Modified profile likelihood inference and interval forecast of the burst of financial bubbles. Quantitative Finance, 17(8), 1167-1186.

Graf v. Bothmer, H.-C., & Meister, C. (2003). Predicting critical crashes? A new restriction for the free variables. Physica A, 320, 539-547. doi:10.1016/S0378-4371(02)01535-2

See also

print.lppls_fit(), summary.lppls_fit(), plot.lppls_fit() and lppls_curvature() for diagnosing the returned fit; lppls_rolling() to recalibrate over a rolling window.

Examples

## A simulated bubble: 200 observations of an LPPLS path whose critical time
## is t = 221, plus a little noise
set.seed(4)
t     <- 1:200
log_p <- eval_lppls(t, A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015, C2 = 0.001,
                    tc = 221, m = 0.6, omega = 8) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.01)

## Calibrate by modified profile likelihood, scanning tc over t = 201..230
fit <- fit_lppls(log_p, fh = 30, mode = "MPL",
                 m_init = 0.5, o_init = 8, num_searches = 2, fp = TRUE)

fit                        # the estimate, and the diagnostics that qualify it
#> LPPLS calibration (mode = MPL)
#>   Window:    n = 200   fh = 30   hold_out = 0   num_searches = 2
#>   Estimate:  tc = 222.98   m = 0.5937   omega = 8.2586   D = 1.034
#>              SSE = 0.0178573
#>   Bounds:    estimate interior;  fits at a bound: m 0/30, omega 0/30
#>   Basins:    SSE 0.0178574..0.0223081;
#>              no distinct inferior cluster (largest gap 0.11 of the spread)
#>   Filters:   B out of range 0   D out of range 0
#>   MPL:       defined at 30/30 tc   MPLE = 223
#>              LI(0.05) [217, 230]   LI(0.10) [218, 229]   LI(0.50) [220, 226]
plot(fit, "fit")           # attached at fit time by fp = TRUE

plot(fit, "mpl_relative")  # drawn on demand
